text:
CITATION
:
Rosenberg v. Minster, 2011 ONSC 4758

COURT FILE NO.:
FC-10-36576

DATE:
2011-08-09

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO

RE:
Jesse
Nathan Rosenberg, Applicant

AN
D:

Arielle Candice Minster,
Respondent

BEFORE:
The Honourable Justice H. McGee

COUNSEL:
J.
Moldaver, for the Applicant

P. Pellman, for the Respondent

HEARD:
August 3, 2011

ENDORSEMENT

[
1
]

The respondent mother brought a motion served July 22, 2011, heard August
3, 2011 for the following relief:

1.

On
an interim basis pending trial, that the Applicant comply with Jewish dietary
laws during his access visits with his daughter;

2.

That
access be suspended during the Jewish holidays with makeup visits provided before
and after the scheduled dates;

3.

Costs
of a substantial indemnity basis fixed in the amount of $7,500.

[
2
]

The applicant father asks that the above motion be dismissed. He also
seeks an order for the scheduling of the Settlement and Trial Management
Conferences.  The scheduling was completed on consent.  Parties are to attend
on October 4, 2011 at 11:30 for a Settlement Conference and on October 18 at
3:15 for a Trial Management Conference.

Background

[
3
]

This young couple was married for 14 months from June 30, 2009 to August
23, 2010.  Their daughter, Chayala was born a few weeks before their first
anniversary.  Ten weeks later they separated.  Mother and child continued to
live with the mother’s parents.  The father established his own residence.  The
mother would not allow the father regular contact with Chayala and he commenced
this application in October.  Case Conferences were conducted on November 29,
2010 and January 10, 2011.  There is no order for custody.  The father’s June
15, 2011 motion for a parenting schedule was resolved.  The terms of that
consent are later set out within this endorsement.

[3]

It is not disputed that much of the post separation conflict arises from
the mother and her family’s expectations as to the manner in which the father
is to spend time with young Chayala.  Both the amount of time he may spend with
Chayala and his manner of care are under intense scrutiny.  The mother and her
family demand compliance with Jewish Orthodox practices which the father
describes as extreme.

[
4
]

The father expresses his religious practice as moderate to traditional.  He
is respectful of the mother’s views.  In turn, he intends that his time with
Chayala reflect his values and expression of Jewish faith.  Father’s counsel
suggests that the true purpose of the mother’s demands is to diminish the
father and to alienate him from his daughter.

[
5
]

Mother’s counsel seeks a two part result: a finding that the parties
agreed to raise Chayala in a strictly Orthodox manner, and an order that the
father be bound to that agreement until Trial.

Analysis

Is a Court to order compliance with a specific religious
practise?

[
6
]

Much of the affidavit evidence in this motion - particularly submissions
of counsel for the mother - focused on the past conduct of the parents and whether
there existed an agreement to parent Chayala in accordance with Orthodox practice.
Whether the parents ever made such a commitment to one another is vigorously
contested, and both parties accuse the other of being disingenuous.

[
7
]

I am unable to make any determination in this regard.  It would require
an assessment of credibility on diametrically opposed affidavits.  More
importantly, it is unnecessary.  It would answer the wrong question.

[
8
]

Section 16(8)
of the
Divorce Act
, states:

In making an order under
this section, the court shall take into consideration only the best interests
of the child of the marriage as determined by reference to the condition,
means, needs and other circumstances of the child.

[
9
]

It is well settled law that where limitation of access is in issue, the
only question to be considered is what is in the best interests of the child.  It
is not for courts to choose between the religious practices of parents:
H.
(B.) v. Z. (S.)

2000 CanLII 26912 (ON CJ)
, 2000 CarswellOnt 4641.

[
10
]

The best interests of a child usually means that a child’s relationship
with the other parent is more important than exclusive conformity with the
religious practices of one parent.
H.(B.) v. Z. (S.) supra
citing
Young
v. Young
(1993) 49 R.F.L. (3
rd
) (S.C.C.)  At page 120 of
Young
v. Young
, the court held that

The custodial parent
does not have the right to determine whether limits should be placed on access.
His or her obligation to make basic child-rearing decisions does not mean that
an access parent of a different faith should not share his or her religion with
a child.

[
11
]

More specifically, Sopinka J states at page 122

The best interests test
should be interpreted as permitting the right to freedom of religious
expression to be overridden only if its application leads to consequences that
are more significant than inconvenience, upset, or disruption to the child and,
to a lesser extent, the custodial parent. The child has the right to have a
meaningful relationship with both parents. Consequently, each parent should be
allowed to involve the child in the different aspects of his or her everyday
life. Parental rights should be shared following marriage breakdown and the
traditional notion of the custodial parent having full control over the child
is no longer appropriate. The best interests of the child test is, in general,
to be applied.
When it is used to restrict religious expression, however,
risk of substantial harm is not only an important factor, but must be shown.

[
12
]

Counsel for the mother acknowledges that giving a child non-kosher food
will not harm the child.  Rather, he suggests that Chayala will suffer
emotional and spiritual harm if she is given non-kosher food in her father’s
home.  Chayala’s age and her parent’s faith system which holds that parents are
responsible for their children’s sins counter this submission.  In the
alternative, counsel paints a picture of maternal distress which will in turn
distress Chayala.

[
13
]

The mother deposes in her July 21, 2011 affidavit that in her opinion
the father’s refusal to be bound by certain dietary and feeding restrictions
“shows a real disrespect towards my religious beliefs and the upbringing of our
daughter.”  Her July 29, 2011 refers to the “devastating effect his
non-compliance would have for me, and I believe Chayala, over the next few
months [until trial.]”

[
14
]

The father denies any lack of respect towards the mother’s beliefs.  Rather,
he chronicles increasingly bizarre demands from the mother and her parents, all
designed to frustrate what ought to be a normal father-daughter relationship.

[
15
]

In my view, the mother’s purported distress is a matter entirely
distinct from a child focused, best interests test.  It does not inform
Chayala’s interests but rather, the mother’s, and whether she is willing, or
able to support an independent relationship between Chayala and her father.

[
16
]

Section 6(4) of the late Professor McLeod’s signature publication,
Child
Custody Law and Practice
is a compelling summary of the fundamental
principal of religious tolerance within Canadian Law.  This principal has been
compellingly articulated throughout every line of the Court’s work.  Within
family law, the principal is soundly settled: the court will only encroach upon
the personal domain of religious freedom, if the failure to do so is shown to
place a child at substantial risk of harm.

[
17
]

“Absent such harm, a noncustodial parent ought to be able to exercise
unfettered access to the children,” paragraph 23:
Fruitman v. Fruitman

1998 CarswellOnt 1941 and at paragraph 24
, “[T]he burden is upon the party who
asserts that “harm” is occurring or likely to occur on the balance of
probabilities.  I am of the view that a court ought to exercise great care and
diligence before determining that “harm” has or is likely to occur by reason of
the exercise of access.  Domestic, custody and access trials are normally
acrimonious and the parties often take extreme positions.”

[
18
]

In my view, there is no evidence that the father’s manner of caring for
and feeding Chayala will place her at any risk whatsoever.  The respondent
mother’s motion that the applicant father comply with Jewish dietary laws
during his access visits with his daughter is dismissed.

Should
the Father’s access be suspended during the Jewish holidays?

[
19
]

Religious holidays are the quintessential markers of faith.  They are
the gatherings, the foundations of familiar affinity - the milestones of a life
lived in accordance with one’s faith.  They maintain traditional practices
while nurturing adaptive and evolving religious expressions.  To exclude a
parent from sharing religious holidays with his or her child, irrespective of
the child’s age, is to tear away at the very fabric of a parent-child bond.

[
20
]

But for the mother’s assertion that she finds the insufficiency of the
father’s religious practices offensive, no evidentiary basis was presented for
the suspension of his access (or as there is no order for access – the father’s
parenting time with Chayala.)

[
21
]

Counsel for the father asks that the mother’s motion to suspend his
access during the Jewish holidays be dismissed.  The father sets out in his
July 28, 2011 Affidavit a chronology of events in which the mother’s claim to
suspend his holiday access is consistent with an overall pattern of
alienation.  Many of the noted events are concerning.

[
22
]

It is not contested that access only started when the father retained
counsel.  Access has been refused for lengthy periods, often only broken by
court attendances.  The issue of Chayala’s diet being restricted to kosher
foods was only raised on June 24, 2011 after other issues interfering with
normalized access were resolved.

[
23
]

Excluding the father from the Jewish Holidays does not appear to have
been raised prior to service of this motion.  In fact, the parties consented to
the following terms which resolved a motion scheduled for June 15
th
:

The father’s
parenting time is to be increased:

1.

On
Sundays from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 a.m. commencing June 12, 2011

2.

On
Tuesdays from 5:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.

3.

On
Thursdays from 5:00p.m. to 7:30 p.m.; to be increased to Friday morning at 7:00
a.m. commencing September 2011

4.

Alternating
parenting time on Statutory Holidays from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

[
24
]

I reflected my view to counsel early in submissions that suspending the
father’s access during the Jewish holidays was not an available outcome.  I
encouraged the parties to attempt to resolve the holiday schedule.  While it
appears that some understandings were reached, the matter did not resolve. At
my request each counsel prepared a draft schedule for the months of September
and October.

[
25
]

I prefer the schedule of the father.  It is a continuation of the terms
of the June 15
th
consent.  Maintenance of those terms place Chayala
with her father on September 29, October 13 and October 20
th

(Thursdays) from 5:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. the following Friday morning.  As there
is already a consent to an order in place for those terms, no further order of
the court is needed.  I therefore dismiss the mother’s motion to suspend the
father’s access during the Jewish Holidays.

Costs

[
26
]

The Applicant has been successful.  Costs submissions limited to three
pages excluding a Bill of Costs and any relevant Offers to Settle to be served
and filed within 20 days of release of these reasons.  Response by the
Respondent 20 days thereafter.

Comment

[
27
]

Successful post separation parenting is an exercise in mutual respect,
cooperation and tolerance.  Divergent views, such as in religious expression,
are opportunities to model these qualities not only toward the other parent,
but within society as a whole.  I would encourage the parties, particularly the
mother, to consider carefully the values that are to shape Chayala’s childhood.
She has two parents and two extended families.  Many resources are available
to assist the mother and father to parent co-operatively.  Chayala deserves no
less.

___________________________

Justice H. McGee

DATE:
August 9, 2011
